questions.question: For an operation $\star$ on $A$, what does the arrow $\star\colon A\times A\to A$ guarantee about the output?
options: Swapping the two inputs never changes the element of $A$ produced.
Each element of $A$ is assigned an ordered pair of elements of $A$.
The output may be any element of a larger set that contains $A$.
Every ordered pair of elements of $A$ is assigned an element of $A$.

questions.question: Why is closure not an extra theorem for a binary operation on $A$?
options: Because closure follows from commutativity alone.
Because every subset of $A$ contains all outputs.
Because the codomain is already $A$.
Because every operation on a set is associative.

questions.question: Does the phrase “binary operation on $A$” by itself say that the operation is associative?
options: Yes. All binary operations are associative by definition.
No, because a binary operation never combines elements of the same set.
No. Associativity is an additional property that may or may not hold.
Yes, but only when $A$ has more than two elements.

questions.question: Why is subtraction on $\mathbb{N}$ a warning example for binary operations?
options: Subtraction is not commutative, since $a-b$ and $b-a$ differ.
Some differences of natural numbers are not natural numbers.
Subtraction on $\mathbb{N}$ is not associative, so it is not allowed.
Subtraction has no identity in $\mathbb{N}$, so it is not an operation.

questions.question: For $\star\colon A\times A\to A$ to be a binary operation, what must it assign to each pair of elements of $A$?
options: exactly one output in $A$
possibly several outputs
an output that may lie outside $A$
no output for some pairs

questions.question: On $\mathbb{Z}$, define $a\star b=a-b$. Is $\star$ a binary operation on $\mathbb{Z}$?
options: Only if $a\ge b$ for every pair chosen.
Yes; $a-b$ is an integer whenever $a,b$ are.
No, because subtraction is not commutative.
No, because subtraction is not associative.

questions.question: On $\mathbb{N}$, define $a\star b=a-b$. Which pair already shows that this is not a binary operation on $\mathbb{N}$?
Let $A=\{0,1\}$ and define $a\star b=a+b$ using ordinary addition. Why is this not a binary operation on $A$?
options: $1\star1=2$, and $2\notin A$.
$0\star1=1$, and $1\in A$.
The operation has two inputs, not one.
$0\star0=0$, and $0\in A$.

questions.question: If $A$ has 4 elements, how many ordered input pairs are in $A\times A$ for a binary operation on $A$?
On $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, which ordinary operation is a binary operation?
options: Subtraction.
Addition.
Multiplication.
Division by the second input only when the second input is zero.

questions.question: For a finite set, what must be true of every entry in the operation table of a binary operation on that set?
options: Every row must contain an identity element.
Every entry must be an element of the same set.
Every element must appear exactly once in each row.
The table must be symmetric across the diagonal.

questions.question: What is the difference between “binary” and “closed” in this context?
options: “Binary” means the set has exactly two elements.
“Closed” means the operation is commutative.
'Binary' means two inputs; closure keeps the output in the set.
There is no distinction: both words mean associative.

questions.question: How many distinct binary operations exist on a set with $2$ elements?
Let $A=\{a,b\}$. A proposed table contains the value $c$ in one cell, where $c\notin A$. What fails?
options: Associativity only.
The number of inputs.
Closure in $A$.
Commutativity only.

questions.question: For $2\times2$ real matrices, which operation is a binary operation on that set?
options: Multiplying a $2\times2$ matrix by a $2\times3$ matrix.
Taking the determinant.
Matrix multiplication.
Extracting the first column.

questions.question: On the set of positive real numbers, define $a\star b=a/b$. Is this a binary operation?
options: No, because division is not associative.
Yes; $a/b$ is positive when $a,b$ are positive.
No, because division is not commutative.
Yes, because division is an operation on $\mathbb{R}$, hence on any subset.

questions.question: Why can a partially defined rule fail to be a binary operation even if its outputs usually lie in $A$?
options: A binary operation must be undefined for at least one pair.
A binary operation must be defined for every ordered pair in $A\times A$.
A binary operation only needs to work for pairs with distinct entries.
A binary operation may have several outputs for one pair.

questions.question: On $\mathbb{Z}$ define $a\star b=a+b-1$. Which element is the identity for $\star$?
options: there is none

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}$, define $a\star b=\sqrt{a-b}$. Why is this not a binary operation on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: Because the rule uses two inputs.
Because square roots can never be real.
Because $a-b$ is always positive.
For some inputs (e.g. $a=1,b=2$) it is not real.

questions.question: On the set of even integers, define $a\star b=a+b$. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a binary operation only when both inputs are positive.
It is not a binary operation because some sums are negative.
It is not a binary operation because the set has infinitely many elements.
It is a binary operation because the sum of two even integers is even.
